Figure 5.1
Stacked bar chart titled "The share of skilled workers in large firms increases with GDP per capita." Vertical axis: "Share of workers (%)" from 0 to 100. Horizontal axis: four categories, "Country income group 1," "Country income group 2," "Country income group 3," and "Country income group 4." Each bar is a 100% stack with six legend categories: gray = Small firms, low skills; orange = Small firms, high skills; teal = Medium firms, low skills; gold = Medium firms, high skills; dark blue = Large firms, low skills; olive green = Large firms, high skills. Visually, the share in small firms with low skills is largest in country income group 1 and declines steadily across groups; the share in large firms with high skills rises steadily and is largest in country income group 4. Approximate visible composition by group: group 1 has about half small-firm low-skill workers, with the remaining half split across the other five categories; group 2 shows a smaller gray segment and a noticeably larger olive segment; group 3 and group 4 are increasingly dominated by medium/large firm and high-skill segments, especially olive green (large firms, high skills). Source: Gottlieb, Poschke, and Tueting 2024. Note states that the figure shows the share of low-skilled and highly skilled workers employed in small, medium, and large firms across four country income categories corresponding to GDP per capita levels of US$0–US$3,000 (group 1), US$3,000–US$10,000 (group 2), US$10,000–US$30,000 (group 3), and more than US$30,000 (group 4). Shares are computed from nationally representative labor force surveys from 76 countries covering 805 country-years. Small firms have fewer than 10 employees; medium firms have 10–50 employees; large firms have more than 50 employees. Workers are classified as low-skilled if they have less than nine years of formal education and as highly skilled otherwise. For countries in each income group, the bars add up to 100 percent.

Map 6.3. Title: "Low-carbon technology jobs in China are growing in manufacturing hubs on the southeast coast, whereas fossil fuel jobs are close to coal mines". Two side-by-side choropleth maps of China with province-level shading and red callout circles/boxes.

The panel emphasizes darker blue concentrations along the southeast/east coast and a few scattered inland hotspots.

Panel b: "Share of fossil fuel jobs, 2019". A choropleth map of China shaded from very light blue to dark blue, with a legend below labeled "Share of fossil fuel jobs (%)" ranging from 0 to 3.75. The same regional labels appear, including BEIJING marked with a star and East China Sea on the right. A large red oval highlights north-central China, with a red label "Shanxi province" pointing into the oval; a smaller red circle highlights the southwest with a red label "Western Guizhou". Darker blue concentrations are centered around Shanxi/north-central China and a smaller cluster in the southwest.

Source note beneath the figure: "Source: Park et al. 2023." Figure 3.7
Scatter plot titled “Low- and middle-income countries are exposed to similar levels of risk from climate change, and they have less adaptive capacity.” The x-axis is Exposure index (higher scores indicate greater risk), scaled from 0 to 0.8. The y-axis is Adaptive capacity index (higher scores indicate lower capacity), scaled from 0 to 1.0. Three country-income groups are shown with colored dots and separate solid linear trend lines: Low-income (dark navy), Middle-income (orange), and High-income (teal). The low-income group clusters mostly around exposure roughly 0.35–0.55 and adaptive capacity roughly 0.65–0.87, with an upward-sloping trend line. The middle-income group clusters mainly around exposure roughly 0.25–0.58 and adaptive capacity roughly 0.35–0.78, with a moderately upward-sloping trend line; one visible orange point lies near exposure about 0.71 and adaptive capacity about 0.50. The high-income group clusters mainly around exposure roughly 0.26–0.58 and adaptive capacity roughly 0.18–0.62, with a nearly flat but slightly upward-sloping trend line. Source note: WDR 2024 team using data from ND-GAIN Country Index (University of Notre Dame Global Adaptation Index) dashboard, University of Notre Dame, Notre Dame, IN, https://gain.nd.edu/our-work/country-index/. Note: The solid lines show the linear relationship for each country group.

initial_ranking.text:
Figure 3.6
Chart title: "In middle-income countries, the weighted average cost of capital for utility-scale solar power projects is substantially higher than the cost in high-income countries." Combination bar-and-dot chart by country, grouped by income class. Left y-axis: GDP per capita (constant 2015 US$), ranging from 0 to 70,000. Right y-axis: Weighted average cost of capital (%), ranging from 0 to 21. Orange vertical bars show GDP per capita for each country. Dark blue circular markers with thin vertical stems show each country's weighted average cost of capital (right axis). Horizontal colored reference lines show income-group WACC averages: low-income (olive), lower-middle-income (orange), upper-middle-income (blue), and high-income (teal). The x-axis lists countries ordered from lower to higher GDP per capita and separated into four labeled groups with slanted divider lines: Low-income, Lower-middle-income, Upper-middle-income, High-income. Visible country labels, left to right: Burkina Faso, Ethiopia, Uganda, Rwanda, Yemen, Rep., Senegal, Pakistan, Kenya, Bangladesh, Ghana, India, Viet Nam, Sri Lanka, Algeria, Egypt, Arab Rep., Iran, Islamic Rep., South Africa, Colombia, Brazil, Bulgaria, Russian Federation, Mexico, Kazakhstan, Malaysia, China, Argentina, Türkiye, Chile, Hungary, Poland, Slovak Rep., Czechia, Spain, Italy, Japan, France, Germany, United Kingdom, Australia, United States. The pattern shown is that GDP per capita increases steadily from low-income to high-income countries, while WACC is generally higher and more dispersed in middle-income countries and lower in many high-income countries, with a few high-WACC outliers. Source note on page: WDR 2024 team using IRENA (2023) and WDI (World Development Indicators), World Bank. Note: GDP = gross domestic product; WACC = weighted average cost of capital.
